- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |

| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |

- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

raw_comment:
Thanks to all teachers and students who responded to our graph on the earning power of college graduates by major.  How much you make in a career isn’t the only criteria for selecting a major, but did this graph change your thinking about your college major and future career?

Lots of questions came up from this graph.  You asked how the majors were selected, how projected earnings were calculated, and how many years is considered a lifetime.  You wondered about what the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentile means and why the blue segments are of different lengths.  But, most frequently, you noticed that education majors made less than STEM majors.  As O'BryantGirlNamedFallon from Boston wrote, “Well, to me it seems like the teachers, who shape the future of our children, are not getting the money they deserve. I wonder, why should the teachers who help all these people reach their dreams, why should they get the lowest pay?” 

Since we continue to post responses, is there more that you notice?  More that you wonder?  Talk to your classmates and read the moderators’ responses. Maybe something they say will lead to more things you notice, wonder, and conjecture. 

Check back on Thursday, January 11 to learn more about this graph. We hope to see you again next month on Tuesday, February 13 for our next "What's Going On In This Graph?"   Signing off now -- Sharon in Boston and Erica in Pittsburgh. See you in February for our special Valentine’s Day graph!

|---|---|---|

- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

raw_comment: This graph does an excellent job of highlighting the different aspect of career choice and the factors that can influence ones decision in deciding which path they choose to pursue throughout their lifetime. On the other hand, it may just be a matter of students tending to choose the career that is most likely to pay more. Overall, the graph is demonstrating that STEM careers seem to be the highest paying, but the reason still remains unknown.

## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

raw_comment:
I notice that many of the higher paying careers are in the STEM fields, while the humanities are generally lower paying. This trend may suggest that, as a society, we value science and technological advancement over fields such as english or history. However, this may prove problematic in the future as science continues to advance without the restraining, ethically-aware forces of the humanities.
In addition, I do wonder about the data in this graph. For example, what constitutes a “lifetime”? For how many years did the people interviewed work in their professions? Knowing this information would aid in understanding the data presented in the graph.
Ultimately, the graph provides statistical information regarding the amount of money people entering different professions can expect to make. It raises the question of what people should prioritize in their career decisions. Should they choose a career that they enjoy despite it providing a lower salary, or should they put their personal interests beneath the necessity of earning money?

raw_comment: I notice that wages seem to be skewed in favor of more technical-oriented professions, such as computer science, medicine, or mathematics, which is interesting since it implies that the more societal-oriented--such as education, humanities, history--are no longer as important. A chemical engineer, from the looks of this graph, would be much better off than a chemistry teacher, even though a teacher would help to serve society through educating the next generations. This makes me wonder, then, how many people actually achieve this profession. How many graduated with a high degree, and how many graduated from a prestigious university? If there are many educators living off a lower pay, and yet a few computer engineers making twice their lifetime earnings, it could be a danger to the distribution of wealth, the welfare of the classes, and the future of the next generations. The story this graph is telling could be that as a society, we have drifted closer to technology than ever before--maybe more than we are to each other, and the well-being of the many.

raw_comment: From this graph, the most clear and alarming issue that should strike everyone’s eyeballs is the educators’ salary. It is outrageous that educators in the United States of America get paid less than philosophers. They are absolutely critical to the education of the next generation. If talented educators leave to get paid more in the private sector, the next generation of Chemical Engineers and other high-paid careers will be far less able. A good educator can truly inspire their students, and it must be difficult for a good educator to fully focus on their job, if they are worrying about making rent or paying for their children’s college education. If this situation does not change in the next few years, I fully expect teacher strikes to emerge, and I will gladly join them.

- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

We look forward to reading your discoveries.
